root_idea.summary: The root is oriented toward movement or agitation; in its communicative branch, a controlled movement or subdued sound functions as an indication.
root_idea.development: The evidence presents signaling as movement of the lips, eyes, eyebrows, mouth, hand, arm, or head, or as a low voice used to convey meaning without ordinary articulated speech. A separate poetic report connects الراموز with the sea, but this does not establish a Quranic form sense.

qac_form_accounting.reason: The canonical Quranic verbal noun is displayed under the normalized citation form رَمْز.

senses.definition: A sign or gesture used to convey an indication, especially communication by bodily movement or subdued sound instead of ordinary articulated speech.
senses.usage_conditions: In 3:41 it describes communicating without speaking normally. The sign may be made with the lips, eyes, eyebrows, mouth, hand, arm, or head, or by a low voice. The same communicative-sign construction includes reciprocal sign-making in a reported variant reading, but that reading is not counted as a separate canonical QAC form here.

other_classical_meanings.definition: To make signs to one another; to exchange indications by gesture or other sign.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: A reciprocal Form VI construction describing mutual sign-making.

other_classical_meanings.definition: A frequent or habitual maker of signs.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: An intensive lexical form for repeated or habitual sign-making.
An idiomatic extension explicitly associated with making suggestive signs with the eye.

other_classical_meanings.definition: An intensive sign-maker, one who makes signs frequently.
other_classical_meanings.usage_conditions: This form is also involved in a reported Quranic variant reading interpreted as people making signs mutually; that variant is not the canonical QAC form displayed above.

lane_unit_coverage.note: Core sign-making and its bodily or subdued-vocal means are covered by the Quranic sense.
Pointer-only cross-reference to the Form I entry.
Frequent or habitual sign-making is represented as a Classical lexical specialization.
The idiomatic sexual-morality specialization is represented separately.
The Quran-linked sign-making interpretation and the intensive sign-maker reading are covered.

cautions: Lane's citation “Kur iii. 36” is retained as a historical citation convention and is not converted into an independent modern verse location; the canonical Quran example uses the QAC location 3:41.
